usage: Most basic connector between two sentences.
I eat. And then I sleep.
I read a book. And I listen to music.
examples: I'm a student. And I'm learning Korean.
I exercise in the morning. And then I go to work.
저는 커피를 마셔요. 그리고 친구는 차를 마셔요.
I drink coffee. And my friend drinks tea.
nuance: 그리고 is the simplest 'and' that connects two full sentences or actions in order. Beginners use it constantly to add a second thought. Unlike English 'and', it usually starts a new sentence rather than sitting in the middle.
mistakes: Trying to use 그리고 to join nouns inside one sentence — for nouns use 와/과 or 하고 instead.
Putting 그리고 at the end of a sentence; it always goes at the start of the next one.

usage: Shows the result of the previous sentence.
I'm tired. So I sleep early.
examples: It's raining. So I'm taking an umbrella.
I'm busy today. So I can't go.
nuance: 그래서 connects a reason to its result, like 'so' or 'that's why'. It points back to the previous sentence and gives the natural consequence. It is one of the first cause-result words a beginner should master.
mistakes: Confusing 그래서 (so/result) with 그런데 (but/by the way).
Using 그래서 to give a command — for commands use 그러니까 instead (그래서 + imperative sounds unnatural).

usage: It's nice. But it's a bit expensive.
by the way / the thing is
But why? / By the way, why?
examples: 이 식당 맛있어요. 그런데 사람이 많아요.
This restaurant is tasty. But there are a lot of people.
I rest on the weekend. But I work on Sunday.
By the way, how much is this?
Changing the topic to ask a question.
nuance: 그런데 is a very common, soft 'but' that can also mean 'by the way' to change the subject. It is gentler than 하지만 and feels natural in everyday chat. Koreans often use it just to ease into a new question or topic.
mistakes: Thinking 그런데 only means 'but' — it very often just means 'by the way'.
Overusing it as a strong contrast; for a clear 'however' 하지만 is stronger.

usage: It's good. But I don't have time.
examples: Korean is hard. But it's fun.
I want to go. But I'm busy.
날씨가 추워요. 하지만 눈이 안 와요.
The weather is cold. But it doesn't snow.
nuance: 하지만 is the standard, clear 'but/however' used to contrast two full sentences. It is a little more formal and direct than 그런데. Beginners can safely use it whenever they mean a plain 'but'.
mistakes: Using 하지만 to mean 'by the way' — that nuance belongs to 그런데.
Placing 하지만 in the middle of one sentence; it starts the contrasting sentence.

usage: I go by bus or subway.
examples: Write with a pen or a pencil.
Two time options for a plan.
nuance: 또는 means 'or' and is used to offer a choice between options, often nouns. It is the clear, slightly formal 'or' you see in writing and notices. In casual speech Koreans also say 아니면, but 또는 is the safe textbook choice.
mistakes: Confusing 또는 (or) with 또 (again/also).
Using 또는 for 'either... or...' emphasis where casual speech prefers 아니면.

usage: Introduces a reason, often paired with 거든요/때문이에요.
examples: I'm not going today. Because I'm sick.
Gives the reason for not going.
저는 한국이 좋아요. 왜냐하면 음식이 맛있어요.
I like Korea. Because the food is delicious.
I open the window. Because it's too hot.
nuance: 왜냐하면 means 'because' and starts the sentence that explains the reason for what was just said. It is often paired with endings like 거든요 or 때문이에요 in natural speech. It answers an implied 'why?'.
mistakes: Forgetting that 왜냐하면 starts a NEW sentence after the result, unlike English 'because' which can join one sentence.
Leaving out the reason ending; natural Korean often pairs it with ~거든요 or ~때문이에요.

usage: Concedes the point but keeps a different result.
It's expensive. Even so, I'll buy it.
It's hard. But still, it's okay.
examples: The weather is cold. Even so, I take a walk.
I'm busy. But still, I exercise.
Keeping a habit despite being busy.
It's a little spicy. Even so, it's delicious.
nuance: 그래도 means 'even so' or 'but still' — you accept the previous fact yet do the opposite of what's expected. It shows a contrast with a feeling of perseverance. It is very natural in daily conversation.
mistakes: Confusing 그래도 (even so) with 그래서 (so/therefore) — they look similar but mean opposites.
Using 그래도 when there is no real contrast; it needs an 'expected vs. actual' gap.

usage: It is raining. Therefore the event is canceled.
examples: The road is jammed. Therefore I take the subway.
There's no time. Therefore I go by taxi.
nuance: 그러므로 means 'therefore' and is the more formal, written cousin of 그래서. You'll see it in notices, essays, and announcements rather than casual chat. Beginners should recognize it and use 그래서 for everyday speech.
mistakes: Using 그러므로 in casual conversation where it sounds stiff — say 그래서 instead.
Confusing it with 그러면 (in that case/then), which sets a condition rather than a conclusion.

usage: I'm busy. But I'll meet you.
examples: 한국어 시험이 어려워요. 그렇지만 열심히 공부해요.
The Korean test is hard. However, I study hard.
I'm tired. But I watch a movie.
It's expensive. But I want to buy it.
nuance: 그렇지만 means 'but/however' and is very close to 하지만, just a touch more formal and literally 'even though it is so'. It contrasts two full sentences clearly. Beginners can treat it as a polite, slightly stronger 'but'.
mistakes: Thinking 그렇지만 differs much from 하지만 — they are nearly interchangeable in most beginner sentences.
Using it mid-sentence; like other conjunctions it starts the contrasting sentence.

english: if so; in that case; then
usage: In that case, what do I do?
examples: You don't have time? In that case, take a taxi.
Is it raining? Then I'll stay home.
이게 더 싸요? 그렇다면 이걸로 주세요.
Is this cheaper? In that case, I'll take this one.
nuance: 그렇다면 means 'if that's the case' or 'then', responding to something just said or asked. It sets up a conclusion that depends on the previous statement. It feels a bit more thoughtful or formal than the casual 그럼.
mistakes: Confusing 그렇다면 (if so) with 그래도 (even so) — one accepts the premise to act on it, the other contrasts it.
Using it when there is no condition to respond to; it needs a 'given that' situation.

usage: Used in past storytelling for the very next event.
I opened the door. Then a cat came out.
I called. And then my friend came.
I turned off the light. And then it got quiet.
examples: 비가 왔어요. 그러자 사람들이 우산을 썼어요.
It rained. And then people put up umbrellas.
I said hello. And then that person smiled too.
I pressed the button. And then the door opened.
nuance: 그러자 means 'and then / just then' and is used when telling a past story, marking the event that happened right after another. The second event is usually someone or something else's reaction. It almost always appears with past-tense sentences.
mistakes: Using 그러자 with present or future sentences — it belongs to past-tense narration.
Confusing it with 그래서 (so); 그러자 marks timing/reaction, not a logical cause.

usage: Marks the next action in a sequence.
밥을 먹어요. 그러고 나서 이를 닦아요.
I eat. After that, I brush my teeth.
I clean. And then I rest.
After that, what do you do?
examples: I exercise in the morning. After that, I shower.
숙제를 해요. 그러고 나서 게임을 해요.
I do homework. And then I play games.
커피를 마셔요. 그러고 나서 일을 시작해요.
I drink coffee. After that, I start working.
nuance: 그러고 나서 means 'after doing that, then' and clearly shows one action finishing before the next begins. It is stronger about order than plain 그리고. Beginners use it to describe routines step by step.
mistakes: Writing 그리고 나서 — the correct form is 그러고 나서 (from 그러고).
Using it when the two actions happen at the same time; it specifically means one after the other.

usage: Leads into an outcome in writing.
I studied hard. And so I passed.
examples: I practiced a lot. And so I got good at it.
I saved money. And so I went on a trip.
We helped each other. And so the work got done.
nuance: 그리하여 means 'and so / thus' and is a formal, literary way to lead into a result. You will meet it in stories, essays, and speeches rather than casual talk. Beginners should recognize it and prefer 그래서 in everyday speech.
mistakes: Using 그리하여 in casual conversation, where it sounds old-fashioned or bookish — use 그래서.
Confusing it with 그러나 (but); 그리하여 gives a result, not a contrast.

english: while doing so; and at the same time
usage: Two things happening together or said with another.
She smiles. And at the same time waves her hand.
I eat. And while doing so, I watch TV.
Adds a remark made during an action.
examples: I listen to music. And at the same time I study.
I drink coffee. And meanwhile I read a book.
My friend smiles. And while doing so, greets me.
nuance: 그러면서 means 'while doing that' and links two actions happening at the same time, often by the same person. It can also hint that someone says or does one thing while doing another. It connects back to the action in the previous sentence.
mistakes: Using 그러면서 for actions in sequence — for one-after-another use 그러고 나서.
Confusing it with 그러면 (in that case); the 서 makes it 'while', not 'if/then'.
